'''Lev Semyonovich Pontryagin''' ({{langx|ru|Лев Семёнович Понтрягин}}, also written '''Pontriagin''' or '''Pontrjagin''', first name sometimes anglicized as '''Leon''') (3 September 1908 – 3 May 1988) was a [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[mathematician]]. Completely blind from the age of 14, he made major discoveries in a number of fields of mathematics, including [[algebraic topology]], [[differential topology]] and [[optimal control]].

==Early life and career==
Pontryagin was born in [[Moscow]] and lost his eyesight completely due to an unsuccessful [[eye surgery]] after a [[primus stove]] explosion when he was 14. His mother Tatyana Andreyevna, who did not know mathematical symbols, read mathematical books and papers (notably those of [[Heinz Hopf]], [[J. H. C. Whitehead]], and [[Hassler Whitney]]) to him, and later worked as his secretary. His mother used alternative names for math symbols, such as "tails up" for the set-union symbol <math>\cup</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Robertson |first1=Edmund |last2=O'Connor |first2=John |date=1999 |title=Lev Pontryagin - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Pontryagin/ |access-date=2023-06-19 |website=MacTutor |language=en}}</ref>

In 1925 he entered [[Moscow State University]], where he was strongly influenced by the lectures of [[Pavel Alexandrov]] who would become his doctoral thesis advisor. After graduating in 1929, he obtained a position at [[Moscow State University]]. In 1934 he joined the [[Steklov Institute of Mathematics|Steklov Institute]] in Moscow. In 1970 he became vice president of the [[International Mathematical Union]].

==Work==
Pontryagin worked on [[Duality (mathematics)|duality]] theory for [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] while still a student. He went on to lay foundations for the abstract theory of the [[Fourier transform]], now called [[Pontryagin duality]]. Using these tools, he was able to solve the case of [[Hilbert's fifth problem]] for abelian groups in 1934.

In 1935, he was able to compute the homology groups of the classical compact [[Lie group|Lie groups]], which he would later call his greatest achievement.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Maritz |first=Pieter |date=2003-06-01 |title=Around the graves of Petrovskii and Pontryagin |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/238845966 |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |language=en |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=55–73 |doi=10.1007/BF02984835 |s2cid=122503334 |issn=0343-6993}}</ref>

With [[René Thom]], he is regarded as one of the co-founders of [[Cobordism|cobordism theory]], and co-discoverers of the central idea of this theory, that framed cobordism and [[Stable homotopy theory|stable homotopy]] are equivalent.<ref>{{citation|title=What's Happening in the Mathematical Sciences, Volume 8|publisher=American Mathematical Society|first=Dana|last=Mackenzie|year=2010|isbn=9780821849996|page=126|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=la0xAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA126}}.</ref> This led to the introduction around 1940 of a theory of certain [[characteristic class]]es, now called [[Pontryagin class]]es, designed to vanish on a [[manifold]] that is a [[Boundary (topology)|boundary]]. 

In 1942 he introduced the cohomology operations now called [[Pontryagin cohomology operation|Pontryagin squares]]. Moreover, in [[operator theory]] there are specific instances of [[Indefinite inner product space|Krein spaces]] called [[Indefinite inner product space|Pontryagin spaces]].

Starting in 1952, he worked in [[optimal control]] theory. His [[Pontryagin's maximum principle|maximum principle]] is fundamental to the modern theory of optimization. He also introduced the idea of a [[Bang–bang control|bang–bang principle]], to describe situations where the applied control at each moment is either the maximum positive 'steer', or the maximum negative 'steer'.{{citation needed|date=August 2017}}

Pontryagin authored several influential monographs as well as popular textbooks in mathematics.

<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Pontryagin mosow.jpg|thumb|right|Monument to Lev Pontryagin on wall of building on [[Leninsky Avenue, Moscow|Leninsky Avenue]] in [[Moscow]], where he lived from 1939 to 1988.]] -->

Pontryagin's students include [[Dmitri Anosov]], [[Vladimir Boltyansky]], [[Revaz Gamkrelidze]], Yevgeny Mishchenko, [[Mikhail Postnikov]], [[Vladimir Abramovich Rokhlin|Vladimir Rokhlin]], and [[Mikhail Zelikin]].

==Controversy and antisemitism allegations==
Pontryagin participated in a few notorious political campaigns in the Soviet Union. In 1930, he and several other young members of the [[Moscow Mathematical Society]] publicly denounced as counter-revolutionary the Society's head [[Dmitri Egorov]], who openly supported the Russian Orthodox Church and had recently been arrested. They then proceeded to follow their plan of reorganizing the Society.<ref name=":0" /> 

Pontryagin was accused of anti-Semitism on several occasions.<ref name=":0" /> For example, he attacked [[Nathan Jacobson]] for being a "mediocre scientist" representing the "[[Zionism|Zionism movement]]", while both men were vice-presidents of the [[International Mathematical Union]].<ref name="NathanJacobson">O'Connor, John J; Edmund F. Robertson "[http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Jacobson.html Nathan Jacobson]". MacTutor History of Mathematics archive.</ref><ref name="Memoirs">[http://ega-math.narod.ru/LSP/book.htm Memoirs], by Lev Pontryagin, Narod Publications, Moscow, 1998 (in [[Russian language|Russian]]).</ref> When a prominent Soviet Jewish mathematician, [[Grigory Margulis]], was selected by the [[International Mathematical Union|IMU]] to receive the [[Fields Medal]] at the upcoming 1978 [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]], Pontryagin, who was a member of the executive committee of the IMU at the time, vigorously objected.<ref name="L1">Olli Lehto.  [https://books.google.com/books?id=1DrQvgK5q9cC&pg=PP1 Mathematics without borders: a history of the International Mathematical Union.] [[Springer-Verlag]], 1998. {{isbn|0-387-98358-9}}; pp. 205-206</ref> Although the IMU stood by its decision to award Margulis the Fields Medal, Margulis was denied a Soviet exit visa by the Soviet authorities and was unable to attend the 1978 ICM in person.<ref name="L1" /> 

Pontryagin rejected charges of antisemitism in an article published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' in 1979.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pontryagin |first1=LS |date=September 14, 1979 |title=Soviet Anti-Semitism: Reply by Pontryagin |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=205 |issue=4411 |pages=1083–1084 |bibcode=1979Sci...205.1083P |doi=10.1126/science.205.4411.1083 |pmid=17735029}}</ref> In his memoirs Pontryagin claims that he struggled with [[Zionism]], which he considered a form of [[racism]].<ref name="Memoirs" />
